text: Ronnie Lee Milsap, born Ronald Lee Millsaps on January 16, 1943, in Robbinsville, North Carolina, is an American country music singer and pianist who was one of the most popular and influential performers of the 1970s and 1980s. Nearly completely blind from birth due to a congenital disorder, he became one of the most successful and versatile country "crossover" singers, appealing to both country and pop audiences with hit songs that blended pop, R&B, and rock and roll elements. His biggest crossover hits include "It Was Almost Like a Song", "Smoky Mountain Rain", "(There's) No Gettin' Over Me", "I Wouldn't Have Missed It for the World", "Any Day Now", "Is It Over", and "Stranger in My House". He is credited with six Grammy Awards and 35 number-one country hits, fourth only to George Strait, Conway Twitty, and Merle Haggard. Milsap was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2014. He was abandoned by his mother as an infant and raised in poverty by his grandparents in the Smoky Mountains until age five, when he was sent to the North Carolina State School for the Blind and Deaf in Raleigh. During childhood, he developed a passion for music, especially late-night radio broadcasts of country, gospel, and rhythm and blues; at age seven, his instructors recognized his musical talent, and he began formal study of classical music at Governor Morehead School, eventually mastering the piano. At age 14, he lost the remaining vision in his left eye after a slap from a houseparent. Inspired by Elvis Presley's 1956 breakthrough, he formed a rock band called the Apparitions with high school classmates and has often paid tribute to Ray Charles, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Presley. He received a full college scholarship to Young Harris College in Georgia with plans to become a lawyer, where he joined the local R&B band the Dimensions and became a regular at the Royal Peacock Club. In 1963, he met Atlanta disc jockey Pat Hughes, who supported his career; his first single, "Total Disaster/It Went to Your Head", sold 15,000 copies with Hughes' radio promotion. He auditioned for a keyboardist role with J. J. Cale and signed with Scepter Records in 1965, recording several obscure singles and working briefly with Ray Charles and Stevie Wonder. That year, he scored his first hit with "Never Had It So Good", which reached No. 19 on the R&B chart, and recorded "Let's Go Get Stoned" as a B-side. In the late 1960s, after moving to Memphis, Tennessee, he worked with producer Chips Moman, became a popular weekly performer at T.J.'s nightclub, and contributed to recordings with Elvis Presley, including "Don't Cry Daddy" (1969) and "Kentucky Rain" (1970), and had a pop chart appearance with "Loving You Is a Natural Thing". He released his debut album, Ronnie Milsap, on Warner Brothers in 1971. In December 1972, after a chance meeting with country music star Charley Pride at Whiskey A-Go-Go in Los Angeles, Milsap relocated to Nashville, where Pride encouraged him to focus on country music. He began working with Pride's manager, Jack D. Johnson, and was signed to RCA Records in 1973. His first RCA single, "I Hate You", peaked at No. 10 on the country chart. In 1974, he toured with Pride and had two No. 1 singles: "Pure Love" (written by Eddie Rabbitt) and "Please Don't Tell Me How the Story Ends" (a Kris Kristofferson composition), which won him his first Grammy. In 1975, he revived the Don Gibson song "(I'd Be) A Legend in My Time" and scored another No. 1 hit with "Daydreams About Night Things". From 1976 to 1978, he achieved seven consecutive No. 1 country singles, including the Grammy-winning "(I'm a) Stand by My Woman Man" and "What a Difference You've Made in My Life". His most significant 1970s success was "It Was Almost Like a Song" in 1977, a piano-based ballad that topped the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart, reached No. 16 on the Billboard Hot 100, and entered the Adult Contemporary Chart at No. 7—his first entry on that chart since "Please Don't Tell Me How the Story Ends" reached No. 95. It was his only crossover success of the 1970s, though he continued to have country chart hits. In the late 1970s, his sound shifted toward string-laden pop ballads, leading to crossover success on the pop charts beginning in the early 1980s. From 1980 to 1983, he scored eleven No. 1 singles. His Greatest Hits album, released in 1980, included "Smoky Mountain Rain", which became a No. 1 country hit and reached the Top 20 on the pop chart and the first of two Milsap songs to reach No. 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart. Other crossover successes included the Top 5 pop single "(There's) No Gettin' Over Me", and Top 20 songs "I Wouldn't Have Missed It For the World" and "Any Day Now", the latter spending five weeks at No. 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart. All four songs reached No. 1 on the country chart. Although the No. 1 streak ended in 1983, "Stranger in My House" remained successful, peaking at No. 5 on the country chart, No. 23 on the pop chart, and No. 8 on the Adult Contemporary chart. "Don't You Know How Much I Love You", released shortly after, became his last significant pop chart entry, peaking at No. 58, though it and others achieved major success on the Adult Contemporary chart, including "Show Her", "Still Losing You", and the Grammy-winning "Lost in the Fifties Tonight" in 1985. Between 1985 and 1987, he had a series of uninterrupted No. 1 country singles, including "She Keeps the Home Fires Burning", "In Love", "Snap Your Fingers", "Where Do the Nights Go", and the Grammy-winning duet with Kenny Rogers, "Make No Mistake, She's Mine". In 1987, he contributed the theme song to the NBC television series J.J. Starbuck. In 1989, he had his last No. 1 song with "A Woman in Love", remaining successful on the charts. Other Top 10 singles between 1989 and 1991 include "Houston Solution", "Stranger Things Have Happened", "Turn That Radio On", a remake of the 1950s hit "Since I Don't Have You" (his last adult contemporary hit), and "Are You Loving Me Like I'm Loving You". With writer Tom Carter, he released his autobiography, Almost like a Song, in 1990. In 1992, he had major success with "All Is Fair in Love and War", which featured rock guitarist Mark Knopfler and peaked at No. 11; his last top-40 country hit, "True Believer", peaked at No. 30 in 1993. By that time, his chart success had declined. Despite this, he remained one of country music's most beloved performers. In 1993, he released True Believer on Liberty Records and achieved a Top 30 country hit with the title track, even as contemporaries were no longer played on country radio. In 2000, his two-disc retrospective 40 No. 1 Hits reached the Country Top 20 and earned gold certification, and his life and career were profiled in a Biography episode. In 2004, he released Just for a Thrill, a collection of pop and jazz standards, which marked a stylistic departure and earned a Grammy nomination. He returned to RCA Records in 2006 with a mainstream country sound on My Life. His two-disc gospel set Then Sings My Soul (2009) reached the Southern gospel charts, and Country Again (2011) reflected a more traditional country style. In 2014, Rolling Stone included "Smoky Mountain Rain" among its 100 greatest country songs. That year, he released Summer #17, an album of nostalgic pop and R&B covers. In 2016, he was among 30 artists featured on "Forever Country", a mash-up honoring the 50th CMA Awards. In 2019, he returned to the charts with Ronnie Milsap: The Duets, featuring collaborations with Dolly Parton, Willie Nelson, George Strait, and others; a duet version of "Smoky Mountain Rain" with Parton reached the Adult Contemporary top 30. By 2020, he had installed a new home studio and continued to record, releasing A Better Word for Love in 2021. In 2022, he contributed "Oh, Lady Be Good!" to Michael Feinstein’s Gershwin Country and launched a podcast, Music and Milsap; that year, he inducted Ray Charles into the Country Music Hall of Fame and was later inducted into the Memphis Music Hall of Fame. His final concert, held on October 3, 2023, at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville, marked the end of his touring career, several months after celebrating his 80th birthday on stage at the Grand Ole Opry. Though retired from touring, he continues to record. Milsap is an Advanced-class amateur radio operator with call sign WB4KCG. In 1965, he married Joyce Reeves; they had one son, Ronald "Todd" Milsap, who was found dead on his houseboat at age 49 on February 23, 2019, from an apparent medical condition; Todd's son discovered the body after not hearing from his father for two days. Joyce, who had been battling leukemia since 2014, died on September 6, 2021, at age 81. On December 2, 2020, six miles of U.S. 129 in Graham County, North Carolina, from Yellow Creek near Robbinsville to the Swain County line, was designated Ronnie Milsap Highway.
